key_terms.meaning: μ<sub>i</sub> = (∂G/∂n<sub>i</sub>) at fixed T, P and other moles; it is the partial molar Gibbs energy.
For each species i, μ<sub>i</sub> in every phase must be equal at fixed T and P.
M̄<sub>i</sub> = (∂(nM)/∂n<sub>i</sub>) at fixed T, P and other moles; the rate of change of the total property per mole of i added.
V̄<sub>i</sub> = (∂V/∂n<sub>i</sub>) at fixed T, P and other moles; the volume contribution per mole of i in the mixture.
Σ n<sub>i</sub> dM̄<sub>i</sub> = 0 at fixed T and P, or Σ x<sub>i</sub> dM̄<sub>i</sub> = 0; partial molar properties are not independent.
The corrected pressure that keeps μ<sub>i</sub> = μ<sub>i</sub>⁰ + RT ln(f<sub>i</sub>/f<sub>i</sub>⁰) valid for real fluids.
φ̂<sub>i</sub> = f̂<sub>i</sub>/(y<sub>i</sub>P) for a component in a gas mixture, φ = f/P for a pure gas; both → 1 as P → 0.
A solution that follows f<sub>i</sub> = x<sub>i</sub> f<sub>i</sub><sup>pure</sup> at all T, P and composition, with zero excess volume and zero heat of mixing.
f<sub>i</sub> = x<sub>i</sub> f<sub>i</sub><sup>pure</sup>; the fugacity of a component in an ideal solution is its mole fraction times its pure fugacity.
M<sup>E</sup> = M − M<sup>id</sup> at the same T, P and composition; it measures departure from ideal-solution behavior.
ΔM<sub>mix</sub> = M(solution) − Σ x<sub>i</sub> M<sub>i</sub><sup>pure</sup>; for an ideal solution ΔV<sub>mix</sub> = 0 and ΔH<sub>mix</sub> = 0.
a<sub>i</sub> = f<sub>i</sub>/f<sub>i</sub>⁰; it replaces mole fraction in μ<sub>i</sub> = μ<sub>i</sub>⁰ + RT ln a<sub>i</sub>.
γ<sub>i</sub> = a<sub>i</sub>/x<sub>i</sub>; it measures liquid-phase nonideality and tends to 1 in the Lewis-Randall standard state.
An excess Gibbs energy model, for example G<sup>E</sup>/RT = x1x2(A21x1 + A12x2), used to obtain activity coefficients.
A two-parameter excess Gibbs model G<sup>E</sup>/RT = A12A21x1x2/(A12x1 + A21x2) for binary activity coefficients.
A local-composition model G<sup>E</sup>/RT = −Σ x<sub>i</sub> ln(Σ x<sub>j</sub> Λ<sub>ij</sub>) used for activity coefficients of miscible mixtures.
For vapor-liquid equilibrium, μ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> = μ<sub>i</sub><sup>L</sup>, equivalently f<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> = f<sub>i</sub><sup>L</sup> for each component.
y<sub>i</sub>P = γ<sub>i</sub> x<sub>i</sub> P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> for low-pressure VLE with ideal vapor and nonideal liquid.
The limit of γ<sub>i</sub> as x<sub>i</sub> → 0; it characterizes dilute-component nonideality and helps fit models.

takeaways: Chemical potential is the partial molar Gibbs energy, and equality of μ<sub>i</sub> across phases is the equilibrium condition.
Partial molar properties describe how a mixture property changes when one component is added at fixed T, P and other amounts.
The Gibbs-Duhem equation ties partial molar properties together, so they cannot all be varied independently.
Fugacity preserves the simple chemical-potential formula for real gases, and φ<sub>i</sub> measures gas nonideality.
An ideal solution follows the Lewis-Randall rule, while real solutions deviate and need activity coefficients.
Excess properties and property changes of mixing show how far a real mixture is from ideal-solution behavior.
Activity replaces mole fraction in the chemical potential, and γ<sub>i</sub> = a<sub>i</sub>/x<sub>i</sub> is the practical measure of liquid nonideality.
Margules, van Laar and Wilson models convert excess Gibbs energy information into activity coefficients for VLE calculations.
bank_note: The syllabi stress derivations and numerical use of chemical potential, fugacity and activity, Gibbs-Duhem consistency, excess properties, activity coefficient models and VLE calculations.

bank.q: Define chemical potential and state the phase-equilibrium criterion for a species present in two phases. Explain why the criterion uses μ rather than concentration.
outline: Definition of μ as partial molar Gibbs energy
Equality of μ<sub>i</sub> in all phases at equilibrium
Derivation from dG at fixed T and P
Concentration alone is insufficient because μ includes standard state and nonideality
answer: Definition. For a mixture of total Gibbs energy nG, the chemical potential of species i is μi = [∂(nG)/∂ni]T,P,nj: the rate at which the total Gibbs energy rises per mole of i added, with T, P and every other nj fixed. It is the partial molar Gibbs energy, Ḡi, in J/mol. For a pure substance it is simply the molar Gibbs energy.
Open-system relation. With moles free to change, d(nG) = −(nS) dT + (nV) dP + Σ μi dni. At fixed T and P this reduces to d(nG) = Σ μi dni.
Two phases. Let phases α and β exchange species i inside a closed vessel at fixed T and P. Whatever leaves β enters α, so dniβ = −dniα and dGtotal = (μiα − μiβ) dniα.

Criterion. At fixed T and P a spontaneous change lowers G, and at equilibrium G is at its minimum, so dGtotal = 0 for any small transfer. Since dniα is arbitrary, μiα = μiβ for every species i, together with equal T (no heat flow) and equal P (no volume change). For π phases: μiα = μiβ = … = μiπ.

Direction. If μiβ > μiα, a transfer from β to α (dniα > 0) gives dG < 0, so species move from higher to lower μ. Example: with μvap = 101.5 kJ/mol and μliq = 100.0 kJ/mol, condensing 0.010 mol gives ΔG = (100.0 − 101.5)(0.010) = −0.015 kJ = −15 J, so condensation is spontaneous.

Why μ and not concentration. μi = Γi(T) + RT ln f̂i, so it depends on the standard state of the phase and on non-ideality, not on the amount alone. Water in air above a pool at 25 °C is at equilibrium with y = 0.03 in the gas and x = 1 in the liquid: the concentrations differ by a factor of about 30, yet μ (and the fugacity, about 3.2 kPa in both phases) is the same. Equal concentrations would be the wrong test.
Conclusion. Phase equilibrium needs Tα = Tβ, Pα = Pβ and μiα = μiβ for each i; equivalently f̂iα = f̂iβ, the form used in VLE calculations.

bank.q: Explain partial molar property M̄<sub>i</sub>. Give the relation between total mixture property M and partial molar properties, and describe one way to measure partial molar volume.
outline: Definition as derivative at fixed T, P and other moles
Relation M = Σ x<sub>i</sub> M̄<sub>i</sub>
Physical meaning of adding one mole of component i
Intercept method on a V versus mole-fraction plot
answer: Definition. For any molar property M (V, H, S, G) the partial molar property is M̄i = [∂(nM)/∂ni]T,P,nj. It is the rate at which the total property nM changes per mole of i added, with T, P and every other nj fixed. Its units are those of M (for example cm³/mol for volume). Ḡi = μi.

Physical meaning. Add a few drops of ethanol to a large tank of water: the volume grows by less than the drops' own volume, because ethanol molecules pack among the water molecules. The partial molar volume of ethanol in that water is smaller than the molar volume of pure ethanol; it depends on the composition of the mixture.

Summability relation. Because nM is homogeneous of degree one in the moles, Euler's theorem gives nM = Σ ni M̄i, and dividing by n gives M = Σ xi M̄i. The M̄i are taken at the actual composition, not the pure-component values.
Binary formulas. M̄₁ = M + x₂ (dM/dx₁) and M̄₂ = M − x₁ (dM/dx₁), at fixed T and P.

answer.text: Tangent-intercept method (worked). For V = 18 + 28x₁ − 6x₁² cm³/mol at x₁ = 0.25:

answer: Reading it on the graph. The tangent to the V–x₁ curve at x₁ = 0.25 is V = 18.375 + 25x₁. Its intercept at x₁ = 1 is V̄₁ = 43.375 cm³/mol and at x₁ = 0 is V̄₂ = 18.375 cm³/mol.

Measuring V̄ in the laboratory. Weigh out mixtures at several compositions, measure each density ρ with a pycnometer or densimeter, and compute V = (x₁M₁ + x₂M₂)/ρ with M₁, M₂ the molar masses. Fit V against x₁ with a smooth polynomial, then apply the binary formulas (or draw tangents) at the composition wanted.
Check. x₁V̄₁ + x₂V̄₂ = 0.25 × 43.375 + 0.75 × 18.375 = 10.844 + 13.781 = 24.625 cm³/mol = V, as the summability relation requires.

bank.q: Write the Gibbs-Duhem equation for a mixture at fixed T and P. State what it says about partial molar properties and give one consequence for activity coefficients.
outline: Equation Σ x<sub>i</sub> dM̄<sub>i</sub> = 0 or Σ n<sub>i</sub> dM̄<sub>i</sub> = 0
Partial molar properties are not independent
For activity coefficients Σ x<sub>i</sub> d ln γ<sub>i</sub> = 0 at fixed T and P
Use in consistency testing
answer: Equation. At fixed T and P, Σ ni dM̄i = 0, or dividing by n, Σ xi dM̄i = 0. For a binary, x₁ dM̄₁ + x₂ dM̄₂ = 0, so dM̄₂/dx₁ = −(x₁/x₂)(dM̄₁/dx₁).

Where it comes from. nM = Σ ni M̄i (Euler). Differentiating gives d(nM) = Σ M̄i dni + Σ ni dM̄i, while the definition of M̄i gives d(nM) = Σ M̄i dni at fixed T and P. Subtracting leaves Σ ni dM̄i = 0.

What it says. The partial molar properties of a mixture cannot change independently: in a binary, if M̄₁ rises with x₁, M̄₂ must fall, and the slopes are in the ratio |dM̄₁/dx₁| : |dM̄₂/dx₁| = x₂ : x₁. Example: at x₁ = 0.40, dM̄₁/dx₁ = −30.0 forces dM̄₂/dx₁ = −(0.40/0.60)(−30.0) = +20.0.
For chemical potential. With M = G, M̄i = μi, so Σ xi dμi = 0. Writing μi = Γi + RT ln(xiγi fi) and using Σ xi d ln xi = Σ dxi = 0 gives the activity-coefficient form x₁ d ln γ₁ + x₂ d ln γ₂ = 0.

Consequence for activity coefficients. Once ln γ₁ is known as a function of x₁, ln γ₂ follows. Take ln γ₁ = 0.8x₂²: then ln γ₂ must be 0.8x₁². At x₁ = 0.30: d ln γ₁/dx₁ = −1.6x₂ = −1.12 and d ln γ₂/dx₁ = 1.6x₁ = 0.48; 0.30(−1.12) + 0.70(0.48) = −0.336 + 0.336 = 0.
Use. Measured γ₁ and γ₂ that break this relation fail the consistency test (point or area test), which catches errors in VLE data before they are used for column design.

bank.q: Define fugacity and fugacity coefficient for a pure gas and for a component in a gas mixture. State the limiting values as P → 0.
outline: Fugacity replaces pressure in the chemical-potential formula
Pure gas φ = f/P
Mixture φ̂<sub>i</sub> = f̂<sub>i</sub>/(y<sub>i</sub>P)
φ → 1 and φ<sub>i</sub> → 1 as P → 0
Fugacity has pressure units
answer: Why fugacity is needed. For an ideal gas at fixed T, dG = V dP = RT d ln P, so G = Γ(T) + RT ln P. A real gas has V ≠ RT/P, so this form fails.
Fugacity of a pure gas. Lewis kept the form and replaced P by the fugacity f: Gi = Γi(T) + RT ln fi, with the condition fi → P as P → 0. f has pressure units.
Fugacity coefficient (pure). φi = fi/P, dimensionless. ln φi = GiR/RT = ∫₀ᴾ (Z − 1) dP/P at constant T. φ < 1 when attractions dominate (Z < 1), φ > 1 when repulsions dominate (Z > 1).
Component in a mixture. μi = Γi(T) + RT ln f̂i, with f̂i → yiP as P → 0. The fugacity coefficient is φ̂i = f̂i/(yiP), and ln φ̂i = ḠiR/RT, the partial molar residual Gibbs energy over RT.
Limits. As P → 0: f → P, φ → 1, f̂i → yiP and φ̂i → 1. For an ideal gas φ = 1 at every pressure.
Example. A gas with Z = 0.90 from 1 to 10 bar (ideal below 1 bar): ln φ = (0.90 − 1) ln(10/1) = −0.2303, φ = 0.794, f = 7.94 bar at 10 bar, about 21 % below the pressure.
Equilibrium use. Because μiα = μiβ, f̂iα = f̂iβ at equilibrium: the isofugacity condition behind every VLE calculation.

bank.q: Starting from μ<sub>i</sub> = μ<sub>i</sub>⁰ + RT ln(f<sub>i</sub>/f<sub>i</sub>⁰), derive ln φ̂<sub>i</sub> = (μ<sub>i</sub> − μ<sub>i</sub><sup>ig</sup>)/RT for a component in a gas mixture, and show how φ̂<sub>i</sub> is found from an equation of state. State each term.
outline: Ideal-gas chemical potential μ<sub>i</sub><sup>ig</sup> = μ<sub>i</sub>⁰ + RT ln(y<sub>i</sub>P/P⁰)
Subtract ideal-gas expression from real expression
φ<sub>i</sub> = f<sub>i</sub>/(x<sub>i</sub>P)
Residual chemical potential relation
Use of an equation of state to compute φ<sub>i</sub>
answer: Real chemical potential. For component i in a gas mixture at T, μi = Γi(T) + RT ln f̂i, where Γi(T) depends on temperature only and f̂i is the fugacity of i in the mixture.

Ideal-gas chemical potential. In an ideal-gas mixture at the same T, P and composition, the fugacity equals the partial pressure: μiig = Γi(T) + RT ln(yiP). The same Γi appears because both expressions must agree as P → 0.
Subtract. μi − μiig = RT ln f̂i − RT ln(yiP) = RT ln[f̂i/(yiP)] = RT ln φ̂i. So ln φ̂i = (μi − μiig)/RT = ḠiR/RT: the fugacity coefficient is the partial molar residual Gibbs energy over RT.

From volumetric data. At fixed T and composition, (∂μi/∂P) = V̄i and (∂μiig/∂P) = RT/P. Integrating from P = 0, where both are equal: ln φ̂i = ∫₀ᴾ (V̄i/RT − 1/P) dP = ∫₀ᴾ (Z̄i − 1) dP/P. For a pure gas, ln φ = ∫₀ᴾ (Z − 1) dP/P.

With the virial equation. Z = 1 + BP/RT gives ln φ = BP/RT for a pure gas. For a binary mixture the same route gives ln φ̂₁ = (P/RT)(B₁₁ + y₂²δ₁₂) with δ₁₂ = 2B₁₂ − B₁₁ − B₂₂. With a cubic equation of state the integral is done analytically in Z.

answer.text: Numbers. n-butane at 500 K and 15 bar, from the Pitzer correlation (Tc = 425.1 K, Pc = 37.96 bar, ω = 0.200):

answer: Terms. Γi(T): temperature-only integration constant; f̂i: fugacity of i in the mixture (bar); yi: mole fraction in the gas; φ̂i: fugacity coefficient (dimensionless); ḠiR: partial molar residual Gibbs energy (J/mol); V̄i: partial molar volume; B: second virial coefficient.

bank.q: For low-pressure vapor-liquid equilibrium, derive the modified Raoult's law y<sub>i</sub>P = γ<sub>i</sub> x<sub>i</sub> P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> and list the assumptions.
outline: Equate fugacities in vapor and liquid
Ideal vapor: φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> = 1
Liquid fugacity written with activity coefficient
Approximate pure-liquid fugacity by P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>
Assumptions: low pressure, ideal vapor, negligible Poynting correction
answer: Equilibrium condition. At the same T and P, μiv = μil for each component, so f̂iv = f̂il.
Vapour side. f̂iv = yi φ̂i P, where φ̂i is the vapour-phase fugacity coefficient of i.
Liquid side. With an activity coefficient on the pure-liquid (Lewis-Randall) standard state, f̂il = xi γi fi, where fi is the fugacity of pure liquid i at T and P.
Pure-liquid fugacity. fi = φisat Pisat exp[Vil(P − Pisat)/RT]: the saturated vapour fugacity φisat Pisat corrected by the Poynting factor for compressing the liquid from Pisat to P.
Full gamma-phi equation. Equating the two sides: yi Φi P = xi γi Pisat, with Φi = (φ̂i/φisat) exp[−Vil(P − Pisat)/RT].

Low-pressure assumptions. (1) The vapour is an ideal gas, so φ̂i = 1 and φisat = 1. (2) The Poynting factor is 1: for water at 100 °C it is 1 at 1 bar (P − Pisat ≈ 0) and still only 1.030 at 50 bar. (3) The liquid is incompressible and the activity coefficients do not depend on pressure. Then Φi = 1.
Result. yi P = xi γi Pisat, modified Raoult's law. With γi = 1 (ideal solution) it becomes Raoult's law yiP = xiPisat.

Using it. Summing over components: bubble pressure P = Σ xi γi Pisat. Example: x₁ = 0.20, γ₁ = 3.125, P₁sat = 0.80 bar gives y₁P = 0.20 × 3.125 × 0.80 = 0.50 bar; with x₂ = 0.80, γ₂ = 1.042, P₂sat = 0.60 bar, y₂P = 0.50 bar, so P = 1.00 bar and y₁ = 0.50.
Limits. The form fails at high pressure, near the critical point, and for strongly associating vapours (acetic acid), where φ̂i differs from 1.

bank.q: For a binary two-suffix Margules model G<sup>E</sup>/RT = A x1x2, derive ln γ1 and ln γ2 and show that they satisfy Gibbs-Duhem.
outline: Use ln γ<sub>i</sub> = ∂(nG<sup>E</sup>/RT)/∂n<sub>i</sub>
Obtain ln γ1 = A x2² and ln γ2 = A x1²
Check Σ x<sub>i</sub> d ln γ<sub>i</sub> = 0
Interpret sign of A as positive or negative deviation
answer: Model. GE/RT = A x₁x₂, so for n moles nGE/RT = A n₁n₂/n, with n = n₁ + n₂.
Differentiate. ln γ₁ = [∂(nGE/RT)/∂n₁]T,P,n₂ = A[n₂/n − n₁n₂/n²] = A(n₂/n)(1 − n₁/n) = A x₂ (1 − x₁) = A x₂². By symmetry ln γ₂ = A x₁².
Gibbs-Duhem check. d ln γ₁/dx₁ = −2A x₂ and d ln γ₂/dx₁ = 2A x₁. Then x₁(−2Ax₂) + x₂(2Ax₁) = 0 at every composition: the pair is consistent.
Check the summability. x₁ ln γ₁ + x₂ ln γ₂ = A x₁x₂² + A x₂x₁² = A x₁x₂(x₁ + x₂) = A x₁x₂ = GE/RT, as it must.

Using the model for VLE. If the pure vapour pressures at this temperature are P₁sat = 100 kPa and P₂sat = 40 kPa, modified Raoult's law gives the bubble pressure at x₁ = 0.30: P = x₁γ₁P₁sat + x₂γ₂P₂sat = 0.30 × 1.480 × 100 + 0.70 × 1.075 × 40 = 44.4 + 30.1 = 74.5 kPa, and y₁ = 44.4/74.5 = 0.596. Raoult's law alone would give 58 kPa and y₁ = 0.517, so the positive deviation raises the pressure by 16.5 kPa.

Meaning of A. A > 0 gives GE > 0 and γ > 1, positive deviation (unlike molecules attract less than like ones); A < 0 gives negative deviation. At infinite dilution γ₁∞ = γ₂∞ = eA = e0.80 = 2.23, so the model is symmetric and suits mixtures of similar-sized molecules.

bank.q: An ideal liquid solution is made at 300 K and 1 bar by mixing 2.0 mol of benzene with 3.0 mol of toluene. Calculate ΔG<sub>mix</sub>, ΔS<sub>mix</sub>, ΔH<sub>mix</sub> and ΔV<sub>mix</sub> for the batch, and explain why ΔV<sub>mix</sub> and ΔH<sub>mix</sub> are zero.
outline: ΔG<sub>mix</sub> = RT Σ x<sub>i</sub> ln x<sub>i</sub>
ΔS<sub>mix</sub> = −R Σ x<sub>i</sub> ln x<sub>i</sub>
ΔH<sub>mix</sub> = 0 for ideal solution
ΔV<sub>mix</sub> = 0 for ideal solution
Link to zero excess enthalpy and zero excess volume
answer: Composition. n = 2.0 + 3.0 = 5.0 mol; x₁ = 0.40 (benzene), x₂ = 0.60 (toluene).
Gibbs energy. ΔGmix = RT Σ xi ln xi = 8.314 × 300 × (−0.6730) = −1679 J/mol. For the batch: 5.0 × (−1679) = −8393 J = −8.39 kJ. Negative: mixing is spontaneous.
Entropy. ΔSmix = −R Σ xi ln xi = 8.314 × 0.6730 = 5.595 J/(mol·K). For the batch: 5.0 × 5.595 = 27.98 J/K.
Enthalpy and volume. ΔHmix = 0 and ΔVmix = 0 for an ideal solution, so no heat flows at 300 K and the volumes simply add.

Why ΔHmix = 0. In an ideal solution the benzene–toluene contact energy is the average of the benzene–benzene and toluene–toluene energies, so breaking like contacts and forming unlike ones costs nothing on balance. Equivalently, H̄i = Hi for every component, so H = Σ xi Hi.

Why ΔVmix = 0. The molecules are similar in size and shape and pack the same way in the mixture as in the pure liquids, so V̄i = Vi and V = Σ xi Vi. Benzene and toluene are close to this ideal; ethanol and water are not.
Check. ΔGmix = ΔHmix − TΔSmix = 0 − 300 × 27.98 = −8394 J for the batch, matching −8393 J within rounding.

bank.q: Low-pressure VLE data for a binary at fixed temperature (P₁<sup>sat</sup> = 80.0 kPa, P₂<sup>sat</sup> = 50.0 kPa): x₁ = 0.20, P = 69.9 kPa, y₁ = 0.407; x₁ = 0.50, P = 81.4 kPa, y₁ = 0.615; x₁ = 0.80, P = 84.1 kPa, y₁ = 0.789. Calculate γ₁ and γ₂ at each point, then test the data for thermodynamic consistency with the Gibbs-Duhem equation.
outline: Calculate γ<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>P/(x<sub>i</sub>P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>)
Calculate both components from data
Apply Gibbs-Duhem point or integral test
Plot or compare ln γ1 and ln γ2
State likely sources of inconsistency
answer: Method. At low pressure γi = yiP/(xiPisat). Then test with Gibbs-Duhem: for consistent data x₁ d ln γ₁ + x₂ d ln γ₂ = 0, which also means ∫₀¹ ln(γ₁/γ₂) dx₁ = 0 (area test).

Excess Gibbs energy. GE/RT = x₁ ln γ₁ + x₂ ln γ₂ = 0.1436, 0.2252 and 0.1436 at the three points. Divided by x₁x₂ (0.16, 0.25, 0.16): 0.898, 0.901 and 0.898. The ratio is constant, so the data follow the two-suffix Margules form with A ≈ 0.90.

Point test. For that model ln γ₁ = A x₂² and ln γ₂ = A x₁² satisfy Gibbs-Duhem identically. Check one point: A x₂² at x₁ = 0.20 is 0.90 × 0.64 = 0.576, against 0.5755 measured; A x₁² = 0.036 against 0.0356. Both coefficients come from one GE function.

Area test. ln(γ₁/γ₂) = A(x₂² − x₁²) = A(1 − 2x₁) = 0.540, 0, −0.540 at the three points, matching 0.5399, −0.0016 and −0.5374. The straight line is symmetric about x₁ = 0.5, so the area above the axis (0 to 0.5) equals the area below (0.5 to 1): ∫₀¹ ln(γ₁/γ₂) dx₁ = 0.90 × [x₁ − x₁²]₀¹ = 0.
Verdict. The data are thermodynamically consistent to within the rounding of P and y (differences under 0.003 in ln γ).

Sources of inconsistency in real data. Errors in analysing y (the vapour sample is the hardest to take), temperature drift, impure components or wrong Pisat, non-ideal vapour ignored at higher pressure, and a still that has not reached steady state. A failed area test (net area more than a few per cent of the total) means the data set should be rejected or remeasured.

bank.q: Compare ideal solution, Lewis-Randall rule and real solution behavior. Explain positive and negative deviations from Raoult's law with molecular reasons.
outline: Ideal solution follows Lewis-Randall rule
Real solutions have γ<sub>i</sub> not equal to 1
Positive deviation: γ > 1, weaker unlike interactions
Negative deviation: γ < 1, stronger unlike interactions
Azeotropes may appear
answer: Ideal solution. Every component obeys the Lewis-Randall rule f̂i = xi fi at all compositions at fixed T and P, with ΔHmix = 0, ΔVmix = 0 and ΔSmix = −R Σ xi ln xi. Molecular picture: like and unlike molecules are similar in size and the unlike contact energy is the average of the like ones.

Raoult's law. At low pressure f̂i = yiP and fi ≈ Pisat, so the Lewis-Randall rule becomes yiP = xiPisat. Example: P₁sat = 100 kPa, P₂sat = 40 kPa, x₁ = 0.30: p₁ = 30 kPa, p₂ = 28 kPa, P = 58 kPa, y₁ = 0.517. The bubble line P–x₁ is straight.
Real solutions. f̂i = xi γi fi with γi ≠ 1, so pi = xi γi Pisat (modified Raoult's law). The sign of ln γi follows the sign of GE.

Positive deviation (γi > 1). Unlike molecules attract each other less strongly than like ones, so each component escapes more easily than Raoult predicts; the total pressure curve lies above the straight line. Example: x₁ = 0.20, P₁sat = 0.80 bar and γ₁ = 3.125 give p₁ = 0.50 bar instead of 0.16 bar. Ethanol + water is a classic case; strong positive deviation gives a maximum-pressure (minimum-boiling) azeotrope, at about 89 mol % ethanol near 78 °C at 1 atm for ethanol + water, and very strong deviation splits the liquid into two phases.

Negative deviation (γi < 1). Unlike molecules attract each other more strongly than like ones, often through hydrogen bonds between them (chloroform + acetone). Each component escapes less easily, the pressure curve lies below the Raoult line, and a minimum-pressure (maximum-boiling) azeotrope can form; mixing is usually exothermic (HE < 0).
Azeotrope test. At an azeotrope yi = xi, so γi = P/Pisat; distillation cannot pass through that composition.
Dilute limit. As xi → 0, the solute follows Henry's law pi = Hi xi while the solvent approaches Raoult's law; both are limits of the same real curve.
Summary. Ideal: γ = 1, straight P–x line. Positive: γ > 1, curve above, minimum-boiling azeotrope possible. Negative: γ < 1, curve below, maximum-boiling azeotrope possible.

bank.q: Derive the Gibbs-Duhem equation from the definition of partial molar properties. Use it to show that activity coefficients in a binary mixture are not independent.
outline: Euler relation M = Σ n<sub>i</sub>M̄<sub>i</sub>
Differentiate and compare with dM expression
Obtain Σ n<sub>i</sub> dM̄<sub>i</sub> = 0 at fixed T and P
Apply to M̄<sub>i</sub> = μ<sub>i</sub> or ln γ<sub>i</sub>
Binary relation x1 d ln γ1 + x2 d ln γ2 = 0
answer: Start. For a total property nM at fixed T and P, nM is a function of n₁, n₂, …. Scaling every ni by λ at fixed T and P keeps the composition, so nM scales by λ: nM is homogeneous of degree one in the moles.
Euler's theorem. For such a function, nM = Σ ni [∂(nM)/∂ni] = Σ ni M̄i.
Differentiate. d(nM) = Σ M̄i dni + Σ ni dM̄i.
Compare. By the definition of M̄i, at fixed T and P the change in nM from mole changes alone is d(nM) = Σ M̄i dni.
Subtract. Σ ni dM̄i = 0, and dividing by n, Σ xi dM̄i = 0 at fixed T and P. (With T and P free: Σ xi dM̄i = (∂M/∂T)P,x dT + (∂M/∂P)T,x dP.)

Apply to Gibbs energy. With M = G, M̄i = μi: Σ xi dμi = 0. With μi = Γi(T) + RT ln(xiγi fi) at fixed T and P, dμi = RT(d ln xi + d ln γi). Since Σ xi d ln xi = Σ dxi = 0, what remains is Σ xi d ln γi = 0.

Binary relation. x₁ d ln γ₁ + x₂ d ln γ₂ = 0, so d ln γ₂/dx₁ = −(x₁/x₂)(d ln γ₁/dx₁). The two activity coefficients are not independent: knowing ln γ₁(x₁) fixes ln γ₂(x₁) up to its value at one composition (ln γ₂ = 0 at x₂ = 1).

answer.text: Example. Given ln γ₁ = 0.8x₂², integrate for ln γ₂:
answer.pre:
d ln γ₂/dx₁ = −(x₁/x₂)(−1.6x₂) = 1.6x₁
ln γ₂ = 0.8x₁² + C;  ln γ₂ = 0 at x₁ = 0  →  C = 0
ln γ₂ = 0.8x₁²
at x₁ = 0.30: γ₁ = e<sup>0.392</sup> = 1.480, γ₂ = e<sup>0.072</sup> = 1.075

answer: Check. 0.30 × (−1.12) + 0.70 × 0.48 = 0: the derived pair satisfies Gibbs-Duhem, and an alternative such as ln γ₂ = 0.8x₁ would leave 0.32 at x₁ = 0.30.

bank.q: Discuss fugacity, activity and the VLE criterion. Derive the general isofugacity condition and reduce it to modified Raoult's law for low pressure.
outline: Equilibrium requires equal chemical potential
Equal fugacity for each component
General relation φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> y<sub>i</sub>P = γ<sub>i</sub> x<sub>i</sub> f<sub>i</sub><sup>pure</sup>
Low-pressure approximations
Final modified Raoult's law
answer: Equilibrium condition. Two phases at the same T and P are in equilibrium when μiv = μil for every i (minimum total Gibbs energy).

Fugacity. Writing μi = Γi(T) + RT ln f̂i in each phase, the same Γi(T) appears, so the equality becomes f̂iv = f̂il: the isofugacity condition. Fugacity, with pressure units, is easier to handle than μ, which has no absolute value.
Activity. In the liquid, ai = f̂i/fi°; with the pure liquid at T and P as standard state, f̂il = xiγi fi, and γi measures the departure from the Lewis-Randall rule.
General relation (gamma-phi). φ̂i yi P = xi γi fi, with fi = φisat Pisat exp[Vil(P − Pisat)/RT].

Low-pressure approximations. φ̂i → 1 and φisat → 1 (ideal vapour); the Poynting factor → 1 because Vil(P − Pisat) is small next to RT. For water at 100 °C compressed to 50 bar the factor is only 1.030, and at 1 to 2 bar it differs from 1 by less than 0.1 %.
Modified Raoult's law. yiP = xiγiPisat; with γi = 1, Raoult's law.
Worked check. At 1.00 bar, x₁ = 0.20, y₁ = 0.50 and P₁sat = 0.80 bar: a₁ = y₁P/P₁sat = 0.625 and γ₁ = a₁/x₁ = 3.125; with P₂sat = 0.60 bar, γ₂ = 0.50/(0.80 × 0.60) = 1.042.

Evaluation. The gamma-phi route needs Pisat, a γ model and, at higher P, an equation of state for φ̂i. It works well below a few bar. Near the critical region the liquid and vapour become alike and a single equation of state for both phases (phi-phi, φ̂il xi = φ̂iv yi) is used instead. Errors from dropping φ̂i grow with pressure and are largest for associating vapours.

bank.q: Compare Margules, van Laar and Wilson activity coefficient models. State their assumptions, parameters, strengths and limitations for VLE calculations.
outline: Excess Gibbs energy forms for each model
Number of parameters for a binary system
Wilson uses local composition
Margules and van Laar are empirical
Limitations for liquid-liquid equilibrium and multicomponent use
answer: Common basis. All three models write GE/RT as a function of composition and get ln γi = ∂(nGE/RT)/∂ni, so the two activity coefficients satisfy Gibbs-Duhem automatically.

Margules. One-constant: GE/RT = A x₁x₂, ln γ₁ = A x₂², ln γ₂ = A x₁²; symmetric, γ₁∞ = γ₂∞ = eA. Two-constant: GE/(RT x₁x₂) = A₂₁x₁ + A₁₂x₂, with ln γ₁∞ = A₁₂, ln γ₂∞ = A₂₁. Empirical power series; easy to fit and differentiate; can show liquid-liquid splitting when A is large (A > 2 for the one-constant form).

van Laar. GE/RT = A₁₂A₂₁x₁x₂/(A₁₂x₁ + A₂₁x₂), ln γ₁ = A₁₂[A₂₁x₂/(A₁₂x₁ + A₂₁x₂)]², ln γ₂ = A₂₁[A₁₂x₁/(A₁₂x₁ + A₂₁x₂)]²; ln γ₁∞ = A₁₂, ln γ₂∞ = A₂₁. Derived originally from the van der Waals equation, now used as a two-constant empirical fit. Good for non-polar mixtures of different sizes; it cannot give a maximum or minimum in ln γ and fails when A₁₂ and A₂₁ have opposite signs.

answer.text: Fitting from one point (van Laar). Azeotrope at x₁ = 0.40, 101.3 kPa, P₁sat = 70.0 kPa, P₂sat = 80.0 kPa:

answer: Wilson. GE/RT = −x₁ ln(x₁ + Λ₁₂x₂) − x₂ ln(x₂ + Λ₂₁x₁), with Λ₁₂ = (V₂/V₁) exp(−a₁₂/RT). Based on local composition: the mixture around a molecule differs from the bulk. Two constants; the energy parameters a₁₂, a₂₁ carry a built-in temperature dependence, and the model extends to multicomponent mixtures using only binary constants. It represents strongly non-ideal miscible systems (alcohols with hydrocarbons) well.

Limitations. Wilson cannot predict liquid-liquid splitting at all; van Laar and Margules can, but poorly. Margules and van Laar constants are fitted at one temperature and do not extend well to multicomponent mixtures. All three are fitted to one binary pair, and extrapolation outside the fitted range can place azeotropes wrongly. For partially miscible systems NRTL or UNIQUAC are used.

bank.q: Explain excess properties and property changes of mixing, and how the signs of H<sup>E</sup> and V<sup>E</sup> indicate non-ideality and heat effects. Illustrate with a mixture at 300 K and x₁ = 0.40 that has γ₁ = 1.60, γ₂ = 1.15 and H<sup>E</sup> = +800 J/mol.
outline: Definition M<sup>E</sup> = M − M<sup>id</sup>
Definition ΔM<sub>mix</sub> = M − Σ x<sub>i</sub> M<sub>i</sub><sup>pure</sup>
H<sup>E</sup> positive means endothermic mixing
H<sup>E</sup> negative means exothermic mixing
V<sup>E</sup> positive means expansion, negative means contraction
answer: Property change of mixing. ΔMmix = M − Σ xi Mi, the change per mole when pure liquids at T and P form the mixture at the same T and P.
Excess property. ME = M − Mid = ΔMmix − ΔMmixid, the part of the mixing change that an ideal solution would not have.

Ideal parts. ΔHmixid = 0, ΔVmixid = 0, ΔUmixid = 0, ΔSmixid = −R Σ xi ln xi, ΔGmixid = RT Σ xi ln xi. So HE = ΔHmix and VE = ΔVmix, but GE ≠ ΔGmix and SE ≠ ΔSmix. GE = RT Σ xi ln γi links excess properties to activity coefficients; SE = (HE − GE)/T.

answer.text: Worked numbers (T = 300 K, x₁ = 0.40, γ₁ = 1.60, γ₂ = 1.15, HE = +800 J/mol; RT = 2494.2 J/mol):

answer: Sign of HE. HE > 0: mixing is endothermic, unlike contacts are weaker than like ones; heat must be supplied to keep T constant, Q = nHE. Here 5.0 mol needs Q = 5.0 × 800 = +4.0 kJ. HE < 0: exothermic mixing (stronger unlike contacts, such as hydrogen bonding between components); heat must be removed, which matters in acid dilution and solvent blending.

Sign of VE. VE > 0: the mixture expands (VE = 2x₁x₂ cm³/mol gives +0.50 cm³/mol at x₁ = 0.5, +1.00 cm³ for 2.00 mol). VE < 0: contraction, as when ethanol and water are mixed. Tank and pipeline volumes based on adding pure volumes are then wrong.

Reading non-ideality. Any non-zero excess property shows a non-ideal mixture. GE > 0 (here 678 J/mol) means γ > 1 and positive deviation from Raoult's law; the mixture is still stable because ΔGmix = −1001 J/mol is negative.
Check. ΔGmix = ΔHmix − TΔSmix = 800 − 300 × 6.00 = −1000 J/mol, matching −1001 J/mol within rounding.

glossary.def: The partial molar Gibbs energy of a species, written μ<sub>i</sub>, which determines its equilibrium behavior.
The contribution of one mole of a component to a mixture property at fixed T, P and other amounts.
A relation showing that changes in partial molar properties in a mixture at fixed T and P are not independent.
A corrected pressure that makes the chemical-potential formula valid for real gases and liquids.
The ratio of fugacity to pressure, or to y<sub>i</sub>P for a component of a gas mixture; it tends to 1 at low pressure.
A solution that obeys the Lewis-Randall rule and has zero excess volume and zero heat of mixing.
The statement f<sub>i</sub> = x<sub>i</sub> f<sub>i</sub><sup>pure</sup> for an ideal solution.
The difference between a real mixture property and its ideal-solution value at the same T, P and composition.
The difference between a solution property and the sum of pure-component properties in the same proportions.
A dimensionless effective fugacity, a<sub>i</sub> = f<sub>i</sub>/f<sub>i</sub>⁰, used in the chemical-potential expression.
The ratio γ<sub>i</sub> = a<sub>i</sub>/x<sub>i</sub> that measures departure from ideal-solution behavior.
For an ideal liquid mixture at low pressure, p<sub>i</sub> = x<sub>i</sub> P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>.
For a dilute solute, p<sub>i</sub> = x<sub>i</sub> k<sub>H</sub>, where k<sub>H</sub> is the Henry constant.
The low-pressure VLE relation y<sub>i</sub>P = γ<sub>i</sub> x<sub>i</sub> P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> for nonideal liquids.
An excess Gibbs energy model that expresses activity coefficients as a polynomial in mole fractions.
A two-parameter excess Gibbs energy model for binary activity coefficients.
A local-composition activity coefficient model with binary parameters Λ<sub>ij</sub>.
The condition in which vapor and liquid phases have equal chemical potential for every component.
A mixture composition at which vapor and liquid have the same composition and cannot be separated by simple distillation.
A check that experimental activity coefficients obey the Gibbs-Duhem relation.
The reference state chosen for chemical potential and activity at a given T and P.
The limiting activity coefficient of a component as its mole fraction goes to zero.
The difference between a real-fluid property and its ideal-gas value at the same T and P.
